doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The no-audition first night at Fat Tuesday
summary: Called by Mario Bauza as emergency replacement, he got hand signals from Dizzy and played tunes he knew.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Did you have an audition with Dizzy?

No. No, no, no, no, no, no. He was, one day he had an engagement in New York. He was desperate looking for his drummer because his favorite drummer wasn’t able to leave Boston because they shut down the city due to a snowstorm and Dizzy had an engagement at a club in New York at Fat Tuesday. So Dizzy, once his drummer told him that he wasn’t able to arrive to New York, he has been looking for drummers. He opened up his phone book and started calling people, calling people, calling people. Everybody was busy and then suddenly into his desperation he remembered, oh Mario Bauza told me about a Cuban drummer. So he called Mario, explained the situation, and asked Mario, © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

“Do you think that that guy you told me is available?” And Mario told him, “Okay, let me call him up, I don’t know if he is available.” Mario called me, I was available, and then Mario said to me, okay — it was very funny because the phone rang and Mario asked me, “Do you want to play with Dizzy Gillespie tonight?” Out of the clear blue that was the question and by that time Mario and I were friends, we were friends, and I told him, “Mario come on, you’re too old for this type of joke at this time.” And then he said, “No, I’m serious.” He explained the situation to me and I told him I wanted to play with Dizzy Gillespie since I was born. So Mario called Dizzy, told Dizzy, “Hey we’ve got the drummer already, he is available, he’s on his way to Fat Tuesday.” So that’s how I [gap]. My English was zero. I remember telling Mario, “Mario, you’re going to be there, right?” Because I needed a translator. And Mario said to me, “No it’s all there. You got it. Boom and he hung up on me. So I don’t know — so it is your problem. So a friend of mine came and picked me up, put the drums in — so I went to the club. We arrived to the club and through my friend who was Jerry Gonzalez, the conga and trumpet player who was a great friend of mine.

When I show him my four fingers it’s straight ahead swing. Now when I show him six fingers that means Afro-Cuban 6/8. That way I do this with my fist — when I see my fist, I close my fist that means stop. And then when I point my index finger to him that means drum solo. Let’s go. That was the audition. No audition. Those were the instructions. Right to the stage I didn’t know the arrangements but this I tell the students, about listening to music, about getting prepared. I was familiar with “Night in Tunesia,” with “Groovin’ High,” with “Manteca,” with “Tin Tin Deo,” “Salt Peanuts.” I knew the tunes. I didn’t know the arrangements, but I knew the tunes.
